claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has favorable plasticity and machinability.
The relatively low hardness and strength of this alloy are governed by suppressed dislocation pinning caused by the absence of nanoscale precipitates or ordered phases.
Controlled heat treatment can introduce nanoscale precipitates or ordered phases into CoCrFeNiTi.
Alloying with phase-separation- or ordering-promoting elements can introduce nanoscale precipitates or ordered phases into CoCrFeNiTi.
Nanoscale precipitates or ordered phases act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Obstructing dislocation motion with nanoscale precipitates or ordered phases increases hardness.
Obstructing dislocation motion with nanoscale precipitates or ordered phases increases strength.
Nanoscale precipitates or ordered phases reduce plasticity.
Nanoscale precipitates or ordered phases reduce machinability.
In the absence of nanoscale precipitates or ordered phases, dislocations move more freely.
Introducing nanoscale precipitates or ordered phases into CoCrFeNiTi will increase hardness and strength relative to the simple solid-solution state.
Introducing nanoscale precipitates or ordered phases into CoCrFeNiTi will reduce plasticity and machinability relative to the simple solid-solution state.

contradictions.description: The boundary restricts the hypothesis to simple solid-solution states, whereas the intervention deliberately creates precipitates or ordered phases, so the modified comparison material is no longer strictly within that stated structural boundary.
Loading is limited to the yield point, but plastic strain at failure requires deformation beyond yield and through failure.
The stated uniaxial loading condition does not encompass machining tests needed to measure cutting forces or tool wear.
